Text.Text: The backroom bill is closed. I retired the poster. If you're still willing to study Tempest Bloom, come by; I'd like to teach it without wondering who'll buy tickets to the damage.
A promising entrance. Now give me rank 50 in Twin Blade to announce. The backrooms aren't kind to an act that hasn't learned its ending.

And tonight's challenger is... well, you. The mop bucket's a poor audience, but it's better than the one six Tempest Bloom adepts have in the fight club backrooms. Beat the six and bring me their bout ledger. I'd like to know who's still buying this bill.
Take my key into the fight club and find the backrooms entrance. The Tilted Visor's where you come afterward. I won't make you bow.

The only act I ever announced twice in one breath. Both blades open outward like petals -- pretty, the crowd sighs -- then the whole shape collapses inward and it's a storm with edges. Done right, it's the finish nobody sees and everybody remembers. Done the way they teach it downstairs, it's butchery with choreography.

Promoters who got greedy and fighters who got tired of my rules. They sealed off the old backrooms -- the door behind the main pit, the one your key fits. Past it, the halls are theirs: pit after pit, no bell, no doctor, no me. Everything you need to hurt is inside.

Undercard material, but don't smile yet. Six of them, and they train on people who can't leave. Any one alone would make a decent show against you. They won't come alone -- that's not the kind of bill it is. Warm up before you go down. I mean that.
Six adepts in the fight club backrooms. Bring their ledger here to the Tilted Visor. I'll keep the good microphone off.
You came up walking and the noise downstairs stopped. That's the review I wanted. The ledger -- let's see who they've been booking to bleed.

Ha. Half these names are fighters I banned for exactly this. You just cancelled six acts and the crowd upstairs doesn't even know it owes you. Take the purse. When you've caught your breath, come back -- the bill goes deeper than its undercard.

Five specialists have added shock gear to the backroom pits. Apparently a losing fighter wasn't entertaining enough. Beat the five and bring me their regulator. I used to think a good announcer could make any show worth watching. I was wrong.
They know what you did to the undercard. Bring the regulator back intact; I want to show it to the people who called me paranoid.

Faster than the adepts and twice as vain. Each one has polished a single petal of the bloom to a mirror shine -- one leads left, one only counters, one throws both blades wide and gambles you'll flinch. Alone, each is a solvable puzzle. In those pits they'll rotate on you like a rehearsed finale. Solve fast.

A ring shock regulator keeps an honest pit honest -- kills the current the instant a fighter goes down. They rewired theirs to do the opposite. Fighter drops, the floor bites them back up. That's how they've been selling half-dead men as comeback stories. Pull it off the wall and the pits go back to being merely lethal.

Because I sold spectacle and somebody else sold blood, and blood outdraws me ten to one on this moon. Promoters moved downstairs, my old sound rig went with them, and half a season later there's a second club under my club. I book the crowd. They book the graves. That ends bout by bout, starting with yours.
Five specialists in the backrooms have the shock regulator. Bring it here after you've stopped their show.
You smell like ozone and somebody else's blood. Beautiful. The regulator -- hand it here.

Look at this butchery -- they bridged the safety cutout with a credit chit. A credit chit. Somebody's whole life ended over five decicreds of copper. You've turned their main card into an empty room, friend. Next time you come in, we talk about the man guarding the deep door -- and that talk happens before you go anywhere near him.

The warden is waiting in the backrooms. Fourteen seasons, no losses. I called every one. Challenge him there and bring me his pit sigil when he's beaten. Take a corner you trust; I've read what happens to fighters who don't.
The backrooms challenge marker calls the warden. I'd take a corner you trust. Beat him and bring the sigil straight here. Don't stop to read the names on the walls.

Fourteen seasons, no losses, and I called every one of his fights from the good microphone. He does the bloom the way a glacier does patience -- slow openings you don't notice until both his edges are already through your guard. When the backroom bill started, they gave him the deep door because nobody would buy a ticket to him anymore. Fear is bad box office.

I've read his whole record and wrote half of it. He learns a lone fighter's rhythm very quickly. Company gives him more to read. I'd take that advantage before giving him another proud entrance to remember.

Every backroom fighter carries a pit sigil -- their license, their name, their tally. His cracked the night his trainer died on his blades, and he kept wearing it broken, which tells you what kind of sermon he is. On my desk, that sigil closes fourteen seasons of business the bill has been trading on. It's the difference between hurting them and unlicensing them.
Call the warden at the backrooms challenge marker. Beat him and bring back his pit sigil.
The whole club felt that. Lights flickered mid-bout upstairs and I knew. Show me the sigil.
Cracked twice. Fitting. You did what fourteen seasons of contenders couldn't. Take your pay and rest. The promoters still in the backrooms won't queue up for a fair bout.
Four promoters still have the payout chit. It records every death they've paid for, and I want it in daylight. Defeat the four in the backrooms and bring it here. No applause for this part.
Bring the payout chit here. If they ask you to name your price, keep walking.

My best students, once. I taught them the bloom for the crowd; the promoter re-taught it for the payout. One announces her strikes the way I announce fighters -- listen and you'll live. One only fights out of corners. The twins finish each other's combinations, so never stand between them. I'd say take them one at a time, but they won't offer, and past the warden's gate nobody comes running when you shout. Keep your company close.
Every purse he paid, signed by hand. He trusts banks even less than fighters. That chit is evidence, and he knows it. Bring it here before he finds someone else to put their name to the accounts.

Not yet. Ask me when the circle's done and I'll tell you about the only act I ever refused to announce twice. Short version to hold you over: the master's final bloom emptied this house once -- fighters, bookies, the boy who sold caf at the door. I sold the tickets to it. That's my share of the bill, and it's why I'm still at this desk instead of retired somewhere with weather.
Four promoters in the backrooms still have the payout chit. Bring it to the Tilted Visor when they're beaten.
Four empty dressing rooms downstairs. You're a wrecking crew with footwork, friend. The chit -- careful. The ink is blood in more ways than one.

His thumbprint, his hand, his numbers. Twenty years I wanted this, and now I mostly feel tired. That's the whole bill cancelled except the headliner -- and before you square your shoulders at me, sit down for the next part. When you're ready to hear about the master, I'll be here. Not selling anything, for once.

The master is in the Private Pit. Call him at the challenge marker and beat him. His last performance emptied a house, and I sold the tickets. Come back afterward. I'd like to announce an ending I can bear to remember.

Then that's the card -- you and two names I'll never get to announce, against the last act on the bill. I'd wish you luck, but I've watched you work; luck is for the undercard. Bring me the only proof that counts. Walk back up those stairs.

He knows his own form better than you will. Don't try to make a better version of his fight. Keep your feet, deny him easy room, and answer the openings you see. If you've brought company, make him watch them too.

Then it's yours. That's not a figure of speech -- the form passes to whoever finishes its keeper, and that custom is older than my club and older than this moon's bad plumbing. You'd walk up those stairs carrying the real Tempest Bloom, the one I used to sell as a miracle at two credits a seat. Be gentler with it than he was. Or at least pick better audiences.
Because I've announced enough lone challengers who never made it back to the microphone. You can go alone. I'd like you to have someone watching the opening you're too busy fighting to see.
The Private Pit has the master's challenge marker. Beat him, then return here. I want to see the challenger walk back in.
The floor stopped humming an hour ago. Fifteen years I've felt his footwork through these boards, and now the building is just a building. Say it, so I can stop holding my breath.
The challenger returns. Alive. That's an announcement I can make without dressing it up. Your pay's here. If you still want to learn Tempest Bloom, I'll teach you. We can keep the lesson between us.
Back to the job.
Put my name on the card.
What exactly is the Tempest Bloom?
Who's running this second bill?
What are these adepts like?
Not tonight, Brask.
Here. Every bout they ever booked.
Run the card by me again.
Five specialists. Done.
How do their specialists fight?
What does this regulator do?
How did the backroom bill get so bad?
I'll pass for now.
One regulator, wiring intact.
Back to the warden.
Then I'll knock. With company.
Who was the warden before the door?
Why bring others? I've done fine alone.
What does the sigil matter?
Not until I've picked my seconds.
The warden's sigil. It's over.
Back to the circle.
Four names. Consider them cancelled.
Who are the four?
What's on this payout chit?
And after them -- the master?
Give me a day first.
The promoter's chit. Signed and everything.
Tell me about the main event again.
Then it's the main event.
Can he be beaten at his own form?
What happens to the bloom when he's gone?
Why are you so set on me bringing company?
Not tonight. This one deserves my best.
The final bloom is finished. He's gone.
